title: Seurat’s dots were meant to mix in your eye, not on his palette
body: In *A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte* (1884–86), Georges Seurat set small dots and strokes of separate colours side by side instead of blending his paints. From a distance your eye merges neighbouring dots into one shade, an effect called **optical mixing**, and Seurat believed it would make his colours more brilliant. In practice, dots of paint side by side only average their light, so they can’t outshine the paints themselves; they can still look brighter than paint mixed on a palette, and contrasting dots tend to shimmer. Critics coined the name *pointillism* in the late 1880s to mock the style; Seurat called his colour method chromoluminarism.

slides.question: Seurat’s most famous painting is built from tiny dots. How wide is it?
slides.explanation: About 3.1 m wide and 2.1 m tall (207.5 × 308.1 cm), and he spent two years on it, between May 1884 and May 1886.

slides.alt: Animation on off-white linen: a close-up of big coloured dots zooms out until they merge into a riverside scene. Red and yellow dots shrink until they read as orange, a brightness scale shows the mix landing halfway, then the painting’s size and dates.

slides.prompt: Step back from the dots until they merge. Try all three pairs: what do blue and yellow dots make?
slides.takeaway: Tiny dots merge into the average of their light: red and yellow into orange, red and green into a dull yellow-brown, blue and yellow into grey, not green. The mix is never brighter than its dots.

slides.alt: Seurat’s A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte: Parisians relaxing on a grassy riverbank in sun and shade, a couple with a parasol on the right, boats on the river on the left, all built from small dots of colour.
slides.caption: The real thing, in the Art Institute of Chicago. Seen whole, the dots dissolve into sunlight and shade.

slides.heading: A name meant as an insult
slides.text: Critics coined *pointillism* in the late 1880s to ridicule the style; today it is a neutral word. Seurat called his colour method *chromoluminarism*, and the movement he started is known as Neo-Impressionism.

slides.heading: His yellow turned brown
slides.text: For the sunlit grass Seurat used zinc yellow, a pigment that was new at the time. It has darkened to brown, a change already showing in his lifetime, and researchers have used studies of the ageing paint to restore the painting’s colours digitally.
